title: Enhancement of exciton radius near a band-gap closing through quantum geometry
authors: Jin-Hyung Choi, Sang-Hoon Han, Young-Kwon Han, Sun-Woo Kim, Jun-Won Rhim, Joshua J. P. Thompson
abstract: Exciton engineering traditionally focuses on modifying semiclassical material properties, such as the effective mass and dielectric screening, while largely overlooking the quantum geometry of the underlying electron and hole Bloch states. This approximation is adequate for many materials but breaks down near a topological band-gap closing, where the quantum metric around the band extrema becomes strongly enhanced. In this regime, Bloch states at different momenta become less similar, reducing the projected electron--hole Coulomb matrix elements and consequently weakening exciton binding. We demonstrate this mechanism in a spin--orbit-coupled Lieb-lattice model tuned toward a topological phase transition. The suppressed Coulomb matrix elements narrow the exciton wavefunction in momentum space, leading to an enlarged exciton radius in real space. This increase in exciton size produces an experimentally accessible enhancement of the weak-field diamagnetic response. Our results show that quantum geometry can fundamentally reshape exciton properties near a topological phase transition, revealing a previously underexplored route for engineering excitonic states.
summary: This theoretical paper demonstrates that exciton properties are highly sensitive to the quantum geometry of Bloch states, especially near topological phase transitions. By analyzing a Lieb-lattice model, the authors show that the momentum dependence of electron and hole wavefunctions suppresses Coulomb interactions, which in turn enlarges the real-space exciton radius. This effect provides an experimentally accessible signature—an enhanced diamagnetic response—that relies on quantum geometry rather than just semiclassical parameters.
main_problem: The study investigates how quantum geometry, specifically near a topological band-gap closing, fundamentally alters exciton properties like their size.
main_result: Suppression of the electron-hole Coulomb matrix elements due to momentum-dependent Bloch states leads to a narrowing in momentum space and a measurable enlargement of the exciton radius in real space.
method: The authors solve the band-projected Wannier equation using a Lieb-lattice model, comparing results obtained with full quantum geometry effects versus simplified unity-overlap approximations.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using a spin–orbit-coupled Lieb-lattice Hamiltonian tuned toward a topological phase transition. Excitons are treated as fundamental excitations whose properties depend on the Bloch states of the underlying electron and hole bands.
key_observables: Exciton radius ($\xi$), weak-field diamagnetic response, projected Coulomb matrix elements ($|\Lambda_{\mathbf{k}\mathbf{k}'}|$), and the Hilbert–Schmidt quantum distance.
important_parameters: Topological phase transition point (band-gap closing), spin-orbit coupling strength ($\lambda_{SOC}$), and momentum separation ($q$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on defining the exciton state via a projected Wannier equation and utilizing covariant derivatives to incorporate Berry connections into the position operator.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate single-particle band structures, Berry curvature distribution across varying SOC strengths, and plots showing the suppression of the form factor $|e\Lambda_{q_{	ext{ref}}, q}|$ as a function of momentum angle $	heta$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the theoretical framework by defining the projected relative-position operator using covariant derivatives. It then applies this to a Lieb lattice, showing how topological transitions modify the quantum metric and subsequently alter exciton size and diamagnetic response compared to semiclassical limits.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete mechanism linking topological band structure features (like Berry curvature) directly to measurable optical properties (exciton size), offering an advanced route for material design beyond simple effective mass theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Overview of the Lieb-lattice exciton. (a) Lieb lattice with three sublattices per unit cell and an ex- citon represented by the in-plane electron–hole relative co- ordinate r = re −rh. (b) Energies of lowest exciton states at λSOC = 0.20. The black line marks the minimum direct single-particle band gap. (c) Single-particle band structure along the high-symmetry path shown in the inset. The ex- citon is formed between the upper and middle bands. The single-particle direct optical gap is approximately 0.8 eV in this case, and the exciton levels lie below this energy owing to the attractive electron–hole interaction.

FIG. 2. SOC-tuned band geometry of the Lieb- lattice model. (a-d) Band structures for λSOC = 0.20, 0.05, −0.05, and −0.20. The colour scale shows the Berry curva- ture along the high-symmetry path, and the labels indicate the Chern numbers of the corresponding bands. As |λSOC| de- creases, the bands become more Dirac-like near the band-gap minimum and the Berry curvature becomes more strongly localized there. Although the Berry-curvature distribution changes substantially, the band Chern numbers remain fixed until the gap closes at λSOC = 0.
